nameStory: This tiny mammal gets its name from its stubby tail, which is noticeably shorter than those of its shrew cousins. The 'northern' part tells us where to find it - across the northeastern forests and fields of North America. Scientists gave it the Latin name 'brevicauda,' combining 'brevis' (short) and 'cauda' (tail) - basically calling it 'short-tail' twice!
description: The Northern Short-tailed Shrew is a mouse-sized mammal with a pointy snout and tiny eyes that spends most of its time underground or under leaf litter. About the size of your thumb to palm, it has velvety gray-brown fur and an incredibly fast metabolism that keeps it constantly on the hunt. This hyperactive little predator is actually one of the few venomous mammals in North America. Despite being smaller than most mice, it's the largest shrew in its genus and packs a lot of energy into its compact body.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Compact body about 3-4 inches long with a distinctively short tail that's less than half the body length. Has a long, pointed snout and tiny black bead-like eyes that are almost hidden in the fur.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Dense, velvety fur that feels like soft velvet when touched. Color ranges from dark gray to brownish-gray, often with a slight metallic sheen that changes as you view it from different angles.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Extremely active and aggressive, constantly moving and making high-pitched chittering sounds. Moves in quick, jerky motions and can often be heard rustling through leaf litter even when not visible.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Tiny four-toed prints about the size of a pinky nail, often found in soft mud or snow. Trail pattern shows quick, bounding steps with the tail rarely leaving a drag mark due to its short length.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Small tunnel openings in leaf litter and shallow burrows under logs or rocks. You might find tiny caches of dead insects or small prey items stored underground.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Lives in areas with thick ground cover - under fallen logs, in dense shrubs, or in loose soil where it can easily dig shallow tunnels and hunt for invertebrates.

habitat: Found throughout New England's forests, from dense broadleaf woods to pine forests, and even in shrubby areas and grassy riverbanks. Prefers areas with rich, loose soil and plenty of ground cover like fallen logs, thick leaf litter, and dense understory vegetation. You'll often find them in the same places you'd expect to see salamanders - moist areas with plenty of hiding spots and invertebrate prey.

seasonality.spring: Very active as they emerge from winter shelters and begin breeding. This is when you're most likely to hear their high-pitched calls and see evidence of their tunneling activity in soft spring soil.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with constant foraging day and night. Young shrews disperse during late summer, making encounters more common as they search for new territories.
seasonality.fall: Busy building up food caches and preparing winter shelters. Their fur becomes slightly thicker and darker, and they may be seen more often during daylight hours.
seasonality.winter: Remain active under snow and leaf litter, creating an extensive tunnel system. Their tracks in fresh snow are often the best way to detect their presence during cold months.

funFact: This tiny shrew produces venom in its saliva that can paralyze earthworms and small prey, essentially keeping them fresh as living snacks stored in underground pantries for later meals!
confusionNotes: Most commonly mistaken for a young mouse or vole, but shrews have that distinctive long, pointed snout and much smaller eyes. Remember: if it has a pointy nose like Pinocchio and seems hyperactive, it's probably a shrew. Mice have blunter faces and relatively larger ears and eyes.
contextualKnowledge: Many people don't realize that shrews aren't rodents at all - they're more closely related to moles and hedgehogs. This ancient group of mammals has been around largely unchanged for millions of years, making them living fossils in our New England woods.
compareHints: As the only Blarina shrew in New England, compare it with other local shrews like the Masked Shrew, which is much smaller and has a proportionally longer tail. The Northern Short-tailed Shrew is notably larger and more robust than other regional shrews, with that characteristic stubby tail being the dead giveaway. It's also much more likely to be found in drier habitats than the water-loving shrews.
